Otolaryngology · published research

Dysphonia

Two reports from a 30-woman sham-controlled study found immediate changes in select voice or laryngeal measures after infrared laser plus voiced tongue-trill exercises, while overall voice-quality measures showed no consistent between-group difference. A separate 15-person randomized pilot reported no short-term effect from PBM alone in professional voice users with muscle tension dysphonia.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two reports from a 30-woman sham-controlled study found immediate changes in select voice or laryngeal measures after infrared laser plus voiced tongue-trill exercises, while overall voice-quality measures showed no consistent between-group difference. A separate 15-person randomized pilot reported no short-term effect from PBM alone in professional voice users with muscle tension dysphonia.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Voice > Behavioral dysphonia and Muscle tension dysphonia categories contain three unique titles, all human randomized reports from Brazil. Two 2026 publications each describe 30 women receiving the same laser-plus-vocal-exercise protocol and likely report different outcomes from one cohort, rather than independent replications. A third pilot included 15 professional voice users with primary muscle tension dysphonia. The small number of participants and short observation periods limit conclusions about lasting clinical benefit.

Human and clinical evidence

Bacelete et al. randomized 30 women with behavioral dysphonia to active or placebo laser before the voiced tongue-trill technique. The active group showed immediate improvement in some measures, including maximum phonation time, vowel cepstral peak prominence, self-perceived phonatory effort, and vocal-fold vibration. Sustained-vowel vocal quality did not differ between groups, and some measures also changed in the placebo-plus-exercise group (Bacelete et al. 2026). A companion report using digital kymography found an immediate change in mean opening in the anterior third of the vocal folds; this is a laryngeal motion measure, not evidence of durable symptom relief (Plec et al. 2026).

A separate 15-person randomized pilot in professional voice users with primary muscle tension dysphonia reported no immediate or short-term effect from PBM alone on the studied voice outcomes (Pecorari et al. 2026). This null pilot is not a test of the combined laser-plus-exercise protocol.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the exact dysphonia categories.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in the exact categories.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two 30-woman reports used an 808-nm near-infrared laser at 100 mW and 1.01 W/cm², delivering 9 J per point for 90 seconds at seven points in one session before vocal exercise. Both reports tested PBM before the voiced tongue-trill technique. The database does not report comparable dose details for the 15-person PBM-alone pilot, so its parameters should not be inferred from the other trial.

Interpretation

The paired reports provide preliminary evidence of immediate changes under one combined protocol, but they likely reuse the same small cohort and measure different short-term endpoints. The separate PBM-alone pilot was null. Independent trials with symptom-focused outcomes and longer follow-up are needed to judge clinical value.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for immediate voice changes when PBM is paired with vocal exercise Very low for symptom relief or sustained improvement from PBM alone
Publications and records3 unique titles (Voice > Behavioral dysphonia and Muscle tension dysphonia).

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two sham-controlled reports use the same 30-woman protocol and likely describe one cohort, leaving only one independent study at that size. A separate 15-person randomized pilot found no immediate or short-term benefit from PBM alone. Larger independent trials should separate light from voice therapy, assess meaningful patient-reported outcomes, and follow participants beyond one session.
